**Sir Keir Rodney Starmer**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-1) (born 2 September 1962) is a British politician and former lawyer who served as [Prime Minister of the United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") from 2024 to 2026. He served as [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") from 2020 to 2026 and as [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom) "Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)") from 2020 to 2024. He was the [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for [Holborn and St Pancras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn_and_St_Pancras "Holborn and St Pancras") from 2015 to 2026. Before entering politics, he was a barrister and served as [Director of Public Prosecutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_Public_Prosecutions_(England_and_Wales) "Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)") from 2008 to 2013.

Born in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), London, and raised in [Surrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surrey "Surrey"), Starmer was politically active for the [Labour Party Young Socialists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Young_Socialists "Labour Party Young Socialists") as a teenager. He graduated with a [Bachelor of Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Laws "Bachelor of Laws") degree from the [University of Leeds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Leeds "University of Leeds") in 1985 and received a [postgraduate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postgraduate "Postgraduate")[Bachelor of Civil Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Civil_Law "Bachelor of Civil Law") degree from [St Edmund Hall, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_Edmund_Hall,_Oxford "St Edmund Hall, Oxford"), in 1986. After being [called to the bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Called_to_the_bar "Called to the bar"), Starmer worked predominantly in criminal defence, specialising in [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights"). He served as a human rights adviser to the [Northern Ireland Policing Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Policing_Board "Northern Ireland Policing Board"), taking silk as a [Queen's Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Counsel "Queen's Counsel") in 2002. During his tenure as [Director of Public Prosecutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_Public_Prosecutions_(England_and_Wales) "Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)") and [head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_prosecutor "Crown prosecutor") of the [Crown Prosecution Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prosecution_Service "Crown Prosecution Service"), he handled major cases including the [Stephen Lawrence murder case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Stephen_Lawrence "Murder of Stephen Lawrence"). In the [2014 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_Year_Honours "2014 New Year Honours"), he was appointed a [Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Bath "Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath") (KCB) for services to law and criminal justice.

Starmer was elected to the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"). He supported the [Remain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Remain_(Brexit) "Remain (Brexit)") campaign in the [2016 European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 European Union membership referendum") and advocated for [a second referendum on Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_referendum_on_the_Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Proposed referendum on the Brexit withdrawal agreement"). He served under [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") as [Shadow Brexit Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Brexit_Secretary "Shadow Brexit Secretary") and, following Corbyn's resignation after Labour's defeat at the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), Starmer succeeded him by winning the [2020 leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2020 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"). As Leader of the Opposition, he moved the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") towards the [political centre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_centre "Political centre") and claimed to have eliminated [antisemitism within the party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_British_Labour_Party "Antisemitism in the British Labour Party"), but was criticised for breaking his leadership campaign pledges. His party made significant gains at the [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2023 United Kingdom local elections") and [2024 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2024 United Kingdom local elections") despite a drop in membership.

Starmer led Labour to a [landslide victory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landslide_victory "Landslide victory") at the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"), ending 14 years of [Conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") government with the smallest vote share of any [majority government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majority_government "Majority government") since record-keeping began [in 1830](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1830_United_Kingdom_general_election "1830 United Kingdom general election"). Under [Starmer's premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Keir_Starmer "Premiership of Keir Starmer"), [his government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starmer_ministry "Starmer ministry") ended [Winter Fuel Payments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_Fuel_Payment "Winter Fuel Payment") for some pensioners, implemented an early-release scheme for prisoners to decrease [prison overcrowding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prison_overcrowding "Prison overcrowding"), and launched a National Violent Disorder Programme following [nationwide riots in 2024](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_riots "2024 United Kingdom riots"). Starmer restricted [visa conditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visa_policy_of_the_United_Kingdom "Visa policy of the United Kingdom"), closed legal migration routes—as outlined in his government's [migration white paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Restoring_Control_over_the_Immigration_System "Restoring Control over the Immigration System")—and launched the [Border Security Command](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Command "Border Security Command") to replace the [Rwanda asylum plan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rwanda_asylum_plan "Rwanda asylum plan"). His government also established [Great British Energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_British_Energy "Great British Energy"), decriminalised [abortion in England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crime_and_Policing_Act_2026 "Crime and Policing Act 2026"), and announced changes to workers' and renters' rights, an increase in the [minimum wage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minimum_wage "Minimum wage") and investment in [a new nuclear power station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sizewell_C "Sizewell C"). In foreign policy, Starmer continued [support for Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine "United Kingdom and the Russian invasion of Ukraine") in the [Russo-Ukrainian war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russo-Ukrainian_war "Russo-Ukrainian war") and [qualified support for Israel in Gaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_and_the_Gaza_war "United Kingdom and the Gaza war") despite [formally recognising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recognition_of_Palestine "Recognition of Palestine") the [State of Palestine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_of_Palestine "State of Palestine"). His government negotiated [free trade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_trade_area "Free trade area") agreements [with India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India%E2%80%93United_Kingdom_Comprehensive_Economic_and_Trade_Agreement "India–United Kingdom Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement"), the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), and focused on improving [relations with China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_Kingdom_relations "China–United Kingdom relations").

[Starmer's net approval rating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leadership_approval_opinion_polling_for_the_next_United_Kingdom_general_election#Leadership_approval "Leadership approval opinion polling for the next United Kingdom general election") began slightly positive but fell over the course of his premiership to an average of −46% by November 2025; an [Ipsos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ipsos "Ipsos") poll that month indicates he was the least popular prime minister since its records began in 1977. Starmer also presided over deepening unpopularity towards Labour and a period of left-wing exodus from the party to the [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales"). Labour saw record electoral losses during the [2025](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2025 United Kingdom local elections") and [2026 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2026 United Kingdom local elections"), which culminated in [a leadership crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Labour_Party_leadership_crisis "2026 Labour Party leadership crisis") and his resignation. Starmer tendered his resignation to [King Charles III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_Charles_III "King Charles III") on 20 July 2026, and was succeeded by [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"). On 1 September 2026, he resigned as an MP, triggering the [2026 Holborn and St Pancras by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Holborn_and_St_Pancras_by-election "2026 Holborn and St Pancras by-election").

## Early life

Keir Rodney Starmer was born on 2 September 1962 in [Southwark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwark "Southwark"), south-east London,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Anon-2024-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-The_Daily_Telegraph-2024-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-4) and raised in [Oxted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oxted "Oxted"), Surrey.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-5)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7) He is the second of four children of Josephine ([née](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Birth_name#Maiden_and_married_names "Birth name")Baker), a nurse, and Rodney Starmer, a [toolmaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toolmaker "Toolmaker").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-8) His mother developed [Still's disease](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult-onset_Still's_disease "Adult-onset Still's disease").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Stewart-2020-9)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-The_Daily_Telegraph-2024-3) She attended St John's Anglican Church in nearby Hurst Green, while his father was an atheist.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-10) He was nominally "brought up [Church of England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_of_England "Church of England")".[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-11) His parents were both Labour Party supporters, and reputedly named him after the party's first parliamentary leader, [Keir Hardie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Hardie "Keir Hardie"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Moss-2009-13) although Starmer did not confirm this when asked in 2015.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-14)

Starmer passed the [11-plus examination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11-plus "11-plus") and gained entry to [Reigate Grammar School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reigate_Grammar_School "Reigate Grammar School"), which at the time was a [voluntary-aided](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voluntary-aided "Voluntary-aided")[selective](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selective_school "Selective school")[grammar school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar_school "Grammar school").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Anon-2024-2)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Moss-2009-13) The school converted into an [independent fee-paying school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private_schools_in_the_United_Kingdom "Private schools in the United Kingdom") in 1976, while he was a student. The terms of the conversion were such that his parents were not required to pay for his schooling until he turned 16, and when he reached that point, the school, by now a charity, awarded him a [bursary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bursary "Bursary") that allowed him to complete his education there without any parental contribution.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-15)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-17) The subjects he chose to study in the sixth form during his last two years at school were mathematics, music, and physics, in which he achieved [A level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_level "A level") grades of B, B, and C.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-18) Among his classmates at Reigate were the musician Norman Cook ([Fatboy Slim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatboy_Slim "Fatboy Slim")), with whom Starmer took violin lessons; [Andrew Cooper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Cooper,_Baron_Cooper_of_Windrush "Andrew Cooper, Baron Cooper of Windrush"), who later became a Conservative peer; and the future conservative journalist [Andrew Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Sullivan "Andrew Sullivan"). According to Starmer, he and Sullivan "fought over everything... Politics, religion. You name it."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7)

## Legal career

After being [called to the bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Called_to_the_bar "Called to the bar"), Starmer worked predominantly in criminal defence, specialising in [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights"). He served as a human rights adviser to the [Northern Ireland Policing Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Policing_Board "Northern Ireland Policing Board"), taking silk as a [Queen's Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Counsel "Queen's Counsel") in 2002. During his tenure as [Director of Public Prosecutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_Public_Prosecutions_(England_and_Wales) "Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)") and [head](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_prosecutor "Crown prosecutor") of the [Crown Prosecution Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prosecution_Service "Crown Prosecution Service"), he handled major cases including the [Stephen Lawrence murder case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Stephen_Lawrence "Murder of Stephen Lawrence"). In the [2014 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_Year_Honours "2014 New Year Honours"), he was appointed a [Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Bath "Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath") (KCB) for services to law and criminal justice.

Starmer became a [barrister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barrister "Barrister") in 1987 at the [Middle Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Temple "Middle Temple"), then a [bencher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bencher "Bencher") in 2009.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Anon-2024-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-The_Daily_Telegraph-2024-3) He served as a legal officer for the campaign group [Liberty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_(advocacy_group) "Liberty (advocacy group)") until 1990.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12) After joining the [Haldane Society of Socialist Lawyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haldane_Society_of_Socialist_Lawyers "Haldane Society of Socialist Lawyers"), he was its secretary[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-BK-19) (1988–92[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-21)), treasurer (1992–95[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-23)) and executive committee member (1996–99[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-24)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-25)). As part of his involvement in the Haldane Society, he joined an academic trip to the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") on the eve of its collapse in 1991, meeting the Russian chief justice [Vyacheslav Lebedev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vyacheslav_Lebedev_(jurist) "Vyacheslav Lebedev (jurist)"), led the society's delegation to [Northern Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland "Northern Ireland") during [the Troubles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Troubles "The Troubles"), and organised the UK delegation to the 14th Congress of the [International Association of Democratic Lawyers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Association_of_Democratic_Lawyers "International Association of Democratic Lawyers") in [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town") in 1996, meeting President [Nelson Mandela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nelson_Mandela "Nelson Mandela").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-BK-19)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-26) Starmer joined the newly founded [Doughty Street Chambers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doughty_Street_Chambers "Doughty Street Chambers") in 1990 and worked primarily on human rights matters.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Stewart-2020-9)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-BK-19)

Starmer has been [called to the Bar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Called_to_the_Bar "Called to the Bar") in several [Caribbean countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Community "Caribbean Community"),[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-27) where he defended convicts sentenced to the death penalty.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7) In 1999, he was a junior barrister on [Lee Clegg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Clegg "Lee Clegg")'s [appeal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeal "Appeal").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-28) Starmer assisted [Helen Steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helen_Steel "Helen Steel") and David Morris in the [McLibel case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McLibel_case "McLibel case"), at the trial and appeal in English courts, also representing them before the [European Court of Human Rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Court_of_Human_Rights "European Court of Human Rights").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-29) Starmer was appointed [Queen's Counsel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen's_Counsel "Queen's Counsel") on 9 April 2002, aged 39.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-30) In the same year, he became joint head of Doughty Street Chambers. In 2005 Starmer called his Queen's Counsel appointment "odd" as he had previously expressed support for the [abolition of the monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republicanism_in_the_United_Kingdom "Republicanism in the United Kingdom").[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-31)

Starmer wrote legal opinions and marched in protest against the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War") following the [2003 invasion of Iraq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Iraq "2003 invasion of Iraq"), and said in 2015 that he believed the war was "[not lawful under international law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legality_of_the_Iraq_War "Legality of the Iraq War") because there was no UN resolution expressly authorising it".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-32)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7) He defended one of the [Fairford Five](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fairford_Five "Fairford Five") who broke into the [RAF Fairford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RAF_Fairford "RAF Fairford") military air base in 2003 and disabled equipment in order to disrupt military operations at the start of the Iraq War.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-33)

## Human rights defender

Starmer served as a [human rights defender](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_defender "Human rights defender") to the [Northern Ireland Policing Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_Ireland_Policing_Board "Northern Ireland Policing Board") and the [Association of Chief Police Officers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_Chief_Police_Officers "Association of Chief Police Officers"), and was also a member of the [Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign,_Commonwealth_and_Development_Office "Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office")'s [Death Penalty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment "Capital punishment") Advisory Panel from 2002 to 2008.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-The_Daily_Telegraph-2024-3)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12) The Northern Ireland Board was an important part of bringing communities together following the [Good Friday Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Good_Friday_Agreement "Good Friday Agreement"), and Starmer later cited his work on policing in Northern Ireland as being a key influence on his decision to pursue a political career: "Some of the things I thought that needed to change in police services we achieved more quickly than we achieved in strategic litigation... I came better to understand how you can change by being inside and getting the trust of people".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Maguire-2020-7)

Starmer represented Croatia at the genocide hearings before the [International Court of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Court_of_Justice "International Court of Justice") at [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") in 2014, arguing that Serbia wanted to seize a third of Croatian territory during the [Croatian War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Croatian_War_of_Independence "Croatian War of Independence") and eradicate the Croatian population.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-34)

## Director of Public Prosecutions

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/83/DPP_Keir_Starmer_in_2009_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-DPP_Keir_Starmer_in_2009_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:DPP_Keir_Starmer_in_2009_(cropped).jpg)

Official portrait as [Director of Public Prosecutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_Public_Prosecutions_(England_and_Wales) "Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)"), 2009

In July 2008 [Baroness Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroness_Scotland "Baroness Scotland"), the [Attorney General for England and Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attorney_General_for_England_and_Wales "Attorney General for England and Wales"), named Starmer as the new Head of the [Crown Prosecution Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crown_Prosecution_Service "Crown Prosecution Service") (CPS) and [Director of Public Prosecutions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_Public_Prosecutions_(England_and_Wales) "Director of Public Prosecutions (England and Wales)") (DPP). He succeeded [Ken Macdonald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Macdonald "Ken Macdonald"), who publicly welcomed Starmer's appointment, on 1 November 2008.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Moss-2009-13) Starmer was deemed to be bringing a focus on human rights into the legal system.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Bates-2008-12) In 2011 he introduced changes that included the "first test paperless hearing".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-35) During his time as DPP Starmer dealt with a number of major cases including the [Stephen Lawrence murder case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_Stephen_Lawrence "Murder of Stephen Lawrence"), where he brought his murderers to justice.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-36)

The United states attorney general [Eric Holder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Holder "Eric Holder") reportedly secured Starmer's support for the extradition of the Scottish IT expert [Gary McKinnon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_McKinnon "Gary McKinnon"), who in 2001 had hacked into US military databases looking for information on [Unidentified Flying Objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unidentified_Flying_Objects "Unidentified Flying Objects") (UFOs), on an interdict that could have led to a seventy-year jail sentence. The extradition was eventually blocked by [Theresa May](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theresa_May "Theresa May") during [her premiership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premiership_of_Theresa_May "Premiership of Theresa May").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-37)

In February 2010, Starmer announced the CPS's decision to prosecute three Labour MPs and a Conservative peer for offences relating to false accounting in the aftermath of the [parliamentary expenses scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_parliamentary_expenses_scandal "United Kingdom parliamentary expenses scandal"); all were found guilty.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-39) Starmer prioritised rapid prosecutions of rioters over long sentences during the [2011 England riots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_England_riots "2011 England riots"), which he later concluded helped to bring "the situation back under control".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-41) In February 2012 Starmer announced that [Chris Huhne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Huhne "Chris Huhne") would be prosecuted for [perverting the course of justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R_v_Huhne "R v Huhne")_,_ stating in relation to the case that "[w]here there is sufficient evidence we do not shy away from prosecuting politicians".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-42)

In 2012 the journalist [Nick Cohen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Cohen "Nick Cohen") published allegations that Starmer was personally responsible for allowing the prosecution of Paul Chambers to proceed, in what became known as the "[Twitter joke trial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter_joke_trial "Twitter joke trial")". The CPS denied that Starmer was behind the decision, saying that it was the responsibility of a Crown Court and was out of Starmer's hands.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-43) When [Jimmy Savile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Savile "Jimmy Savile")'s sexual abuse crimes were exposed in 2012, Starmer said amid [the subsequent scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Savile_sexual_abuse_scandal "Jimmy Savile sexual abuse scandal") that "It was like a dam had bust and people rightfully wanted to know why he had been allowed to get away with it for so long."[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-44) In 2013 Starmer announced changes to how sexual abuse investigations were to be handled amid [Operation Yewtree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Yewtree "Operation Yewtree"), including a panel to review complaints.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-46)

Starmer stepped down as Director of Public Prosecutions in November 2013, and was succeeded by [Alison Saunders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alison_Saunders "Alison Saunders").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-48) Starmer was awarded several honorary degrees between 2011 and 2014, and was appointed [Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Knight_Commander_of_the_Order_of_the_Bath "Knight Commander of the Order of the Bath") (KCB) in the [2014 New Year Honours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_New_Year_Honours "2014 New Year Honours") for "services to law and criminal justice".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-Atwal-2013-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-The_London_Gazette-2013-50)

## Member of Parliament

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/62/Official_portrait_of_Keir_Starmer_crop_2.jpg/250px-Official_portrait_of_Keir_Starmer_crop_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Official_portrait_of_Keir_Starmer_crop_2.jpg)

Official portrait as MP, 2017

> My predecessor, the Right Hon. Frank Dobson, to whom I pay tribute, was a powerful advocate of the rights of everyone in Holborn and St Pancras throughout his highly distinguished parliamentary career. Widely respected and widely regarded, he served the people of Holborn and St Pancras for 36 years. Although I doubt I will clock up 36 years, I intend to follow in Frank Dobson's footsteps—albeit my jokes are likely to seem tame when compared with his, and I might give the beard a miss.

—Keir Starmer in his [maiden speech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maiden_speech "Maiden speech") to the House of Commons, May 2015

Starmer was selected in December 2014 as the Labour parliamentary candidate for the [constituency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_constituencies "United Kingdom constituencies") of [Holborn and St Pancras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holborn_and_St_Pancras "Holborn and St Pancras"), a Labour [safe seat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safe_seat "Safe seat"), following the decision of [Frank Dobson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Dobson "Frank Dobson"), its sitting MP, to retire.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-51) Starmer was elected at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election") with a majority of 17,048 (receiving 52.9 per cent of the vote).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-52) He was returned at the [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election") with an increased majority of 30,509 (70.1 per cent) at the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election") with a reduced majority of 27,763 (64.9 per cent), and at the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election") with a further reduced majority of 18,884 (48.9 per cent).

During the [2016 European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 European Union membership referendum"), Starmer supported the [Britain Stronger in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britain_Stronger_in_Europe "Britain Stronger in Europe") campaign for the UK to remain in the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union") (EU).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-53) A member of the parliamentary groups [Labour Friends of Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Friends_of_Israel "Labour Friends of Israel") and [Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Friends_of_Palestine_and_the_Middle_East "Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East"),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-54) Starmer was urged by a number of activists to stand in the [2015 Labour Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)") following the resignation of [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") as [Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") after Labour's defeat at the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"); he ruled this out, citing his relative lack of political experience at the time.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-56) During the leadership election Starmer supported [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), who finished second to [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn").[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-57)

## Shadow portfolios

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Revealing_Brexit_documents_%2849188334841%29.jpg/250px-Revealing_Brexit_documents_%2849188334841%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Revealing_Brexit_documents_(49188334841).jpg)

Starmer and Jeremy Corbyn, 6 December 2019

Starmer was appointed to [Corbyn's Shadow Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbyn's_shadow_cabinet "Corbyn's shadow cabinet") as Shadow Home Office Minister in September 2015. resignations") in protest at [Corbyn's leadership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corbyn's_leadership "Corbyn's leadership") following the 2016 EU Referendum result.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-59) Following [Corbyn's re-election as leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)") in September 2016, Starmer accepted a new post from Corbyn as [Shadow Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_Exiting_the_European_Union "Shadow Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-60) In this role, Starmer questioned May and [her first ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_May_ministry "First May policies put forward at the general election, later saying in 2024 that he was "certain that we would lose the 2019 election".[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-63)

election (UK)").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-65) He gained support from the former Labour prime minister [Gordon Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Brown "Gordon Brown") and [London Mayor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Mayor "London Mayor")[Sadiq Khan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sadiq_Khan "Sadiq Khan").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-winner-66) During the Labour leadership campaign, Starmer ran a [left-wing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Left-wing "Left-wing") platform and positioned himself in opposition to "Anti-austerity")".[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-New_European2-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-68) He indicated he would continue with the I want to pay tribute to Jeremy Corbyn, who led our party through some really difficult times, who energised our movement and who's a friend as well as a colleague. And to all of our members, supporters and affiliates I say this: whether you voted for me or not I will represent you, I will listen to you and I will bring our party together.

—Keir Starmer's acceptance speech, April 2020

## Leader of the Opposition (2020–2024)

Main article: [Keir Starmer as Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer_as_Leader_of_the_Opposition "Keir Starmer as Leader of the Opposition")

Having become Leader of the Opposition during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), Starmer said in his acceptance speech that he would refrain from "scoring party political points" and would work with the Government "in the national [Partygate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partygate "Partygate") scandal.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-73) On 13 December 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom, Starmer recorded a Christmas message at [Waheed Alli, Baron Alli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waheed_Alli,_Baron_Alli "Waheed Alli, Baron Alli")'s house, urging the public to [work from home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Work_from_home "Work from home"), while giving the impression he was in his own home, with a family picture behind him.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-74) In May 2022, Starmer said he would resign were he to receive a [fixed penalty by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Hartlepool_by-election "2021 Hartlepool by-election") and [local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2021 United Kingdom local elections") the previous year.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-75) The controversy surrounding the event was dubbed strikes").[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-87)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-88)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keir_Starmer#cite_note-89)

The **2020 Labour Party leadership election** was triggered after [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") announced his intention to resign as [the leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") of the [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") following the party's defeat at the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"). It was won by Sir Keir Starmer, who received 56.2 per cent of the vote on the first round and went on to become [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_United_Kingdom "Prime Minister of the United Kingdom") after winning the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election"). It was held alongside the [deputy leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_deputy_leadership_election "2020 Labour Party deputy leadership election"), in which [Angela Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Rayner "Angela Rayner") was elected to succeed [Tom Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Watson,_Baron_Watson_of_Wyre_Forest "Tom Watson, Baron Watson of Wyre Forest") as [deputy leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)") after Watson retired from Parliament in November 2019, in advance of the election.

See also: [Labour Party leadership of Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_leadership_of_Jeremy_Corbyn "Labour Party leadership of Jeremy Corbyn")

[Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") was elected Labour Party leader in a [2015 leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)"), succeeding [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") after he resigned following the party's defeat at [the general election that year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), and [re-elected leader in 2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)") following a challenge from [Owen Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Owen_Smith "Owen Smith"). While Labour gained 30 seats in the [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), it lost 60 seats in the [2019 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), resulting in the party having its fewest seats in the [House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Commons_of_the_United_Kingdom "House of Commons of the United Kingdom") since [1935](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1935_United_Kingdom_general_election "1935 United Kingdom general election").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-3)

Former Labour Prime Minister [Tony Blair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Blair "Tony Blair") said that Corbyn's [Brexit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit "Brexit") policy "alienated both sides of the debate" and that he personified "a brand of quasi-revolutionary socialism — mixing [far-left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-left "Far-left") economic policy with deep hostility to Western foreign policy". Blair also highlighted the [handling of antisemitism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_British_Labour_Party "Antisemitism in the British Labour Party") in the party as a key issue.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-4) Political scientist [John Curtice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Curtice "John Curtice") said that "the bond between Labour and its traditional [working-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working-class "Working-class") base is now badly strained" after a substantial swing of votes from Labour to the [Conservatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") in leave-voting areas.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5)

Corbyn took responsibility for the defeat but said he remained proud of his party's campaign.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2019GEmanifesto-6) In _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_, Corbyn claimed that Labour's election campaign had successfully re-set the terms of debate and his manifesto would be seen as "historically important".[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2019GEmanifesto-6) Corbyn's Shadow Chancellor and ally [John McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McDonnell "John McDonnell") also took responsibility for the defeat but also cited the media's portrayal of Corbyn as a factor in the defeat.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-2019GEmanifesto-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Ione_Wells-7) Corbyn subsequently announced that he would resign as Labour Party leader following a "process of reflection".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-9)

## Procedure

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Procedure")]

The election was conducted under a pure [one member, one vote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_member,_one_vote "One member, one vote") (OMOV) system, using the [instant-runoff voting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instant-runoff_voting "Instant-runoff voting") electoral system with preferential balloting to calculate the result.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-next_leader-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Politics-rules-11) Votes were cast using postal ballots and online voting forms. Candidates were elected by members and registered and affiliated supporters, who all received a maximum of one vote, and all votes were weighted equally. This meant that, for example, members of Labour-affiliated trades unions needed to register as affiliated Labour supporters to vote.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-12) Members who joined before 20 January were eligible to vote.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Politics-rules-11)

To stand, candidates needed to be nominated by at least 10 per cent of the combined membership of the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") (PLP) and [European Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliamentary_Labour_Party "European Parliamentary Labour Party") (EPLP), meaning 22 MPs and MEPs at the time. As a result, a maximum of nine candidates could stand. They also needed to be nominated by at least 5 per cent of [Constituency Labour Parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Parties "Constituency Labour Parties") (CLPs), meaning at least 33 CLPs, or at least three party affiliates that consist of at least 5 per cent of affiliate members including at least two trades unions.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-next_leader-10)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-NS-rules-13) Affiliates consist of [affiliated trades unions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK)_affiliated_trade_union "Labour Party (UK) affiliated trade union") and [socialist societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Socialist_societies "Socialist societies").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-NS-rules-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-14)

The timetable for the election was set by the party's [National Executive Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Executive_Committee_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "National Executive Committee of the Labour Party (UK)") (NEC) on 6 January 2020.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-15)

Nominations from the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party") and [European Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Parliamentary_Labour_Party "European Parliamentary Labour Party") opened on 7 January and closed on 13 January. Between 15 January and 15 February, [constituency parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Party "Constituency Labour Party") and affiliate organisations could nominate their preferred candidate. Applications to become a registered supporter opened on 14 January and closed on 16 January. Voting in the membership ballot opened on 24 February[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-16) and closed at midday on 2 April. The result of the leadership election was announced on 4 April.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-4_April-17) The [special conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_conference "Party conference") planned for the announcement of the election result was "scaled-back" on 12 March because of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-AnnoCancel-18)

## Campaign

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Campaign")]

### Announcements

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Announcements")]

Immediately following the 2019 general election, Keir Starmer, the [Shadow Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_Exiting_the_European_Union "Shadow Secretary of State for Exiting the European Union"), was considered favourite to win the leadership election by the online gambling company [Betfair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betfair "Betfair").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-20)[Rebecca Long-Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Long-Bailey "Rebecca Long-Bailey"), the shadow business secretary, was considered another front runner.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-21) Various other figures were considered as possible leadership candidates, including [Lisa Nandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Nandy "Lisa Nandy"), the MP for [Wigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigan_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Wigan (UK Parliament constituency)"), who said on 15 December 2019 that she was "seriously thinking" about standing for the leadership.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Honeycombe-Foster-22) On 29 December, Long-Bailey wrote an article for _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_ declaring her interest in standing and laying out her strategy for a "progressive patriotism".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-23)

Some party figures, including the former MP [Caroline Flint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caroline_Flint "Caroline Flint") and the MP [Wes Streeting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wes_Streeting "Wes Streeting"), argued for a "clean break" from the previous leadership. However, [Len McCluskey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Len_McCluskey "Len McCluskey"), general secretary of [Unite the Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unite_the_Union "Unite the Union"), said that the next leader should "carry on the tradition", describing Long-Bailey and [Angela Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Rayner "Angela Rayner") as his preferred candidates.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-25) Party figures affiliated with Long-Bailey and MPs such as Corbyn, as well as centrist figures like [Alastair Campbell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alastair_Campbell "Alastair Campbell"), encouraged supporters of their preferred candidates to join the party to vote in the leadership election.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-27)[Roy Hattersley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roy_Hattersley "Roy Hattersley"), a former deputy leader of the party, wrote on 21 December that MPs should refuse to accept Long-Bailey if she were elected leader.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-auto-28)

The shadow foreign secretary, [Emily Thornberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Thornberry "Emily Thornberry"), was the first to announce, on 18 December, that she was standing for the leadership.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-29) She laid out her pitch in an article for _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-30) She said that her first priority would be to deal with [antisemitism in the party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antisemitism_in_the_UK_Labour_Party "Antisemitism in the UK Labour Party") by implementing recommendations from the [Board of Deputies of British Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_Deputies_of_British_Jews "Board of Deputies of British Jews"), the [Jewish Labour Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewish_Labour_Movement "Jewish Labour Movement") and the [Equality and Human Rights Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equality_and_Human_Rights_Commission "Equality and Human Rights Commission").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-31) She criticised Corbyn's senior advisers for overruling her as the [shadow foreign secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_foreign_secretary "Shadow foreign secretary") and for their strategic decisions in the 2019 general election.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-33)

[Clive Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clive_Lewis_(politician) "Clive Lewis (politician)"), the shadow minister for sustainable economics, announced on 19 December that he would stand.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-34) He said that as leader, he would give more democratic power in the party to its members.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-35) He argued that the party should work more with other political parties on the left, and proposed constitutional reforms including supporting [proportional representation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_representation "Proportional representation") and [reform of the House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_of_the_House_of_Lords "Reform of the House of Lords").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-37) In January 2020, he proposed a referendum about the future of the [British royal family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_royal_family "British royal family").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-38) He was criticised for his response to claims against him of sexual harassment, for which he had been cleared by a disciplinary body within Labour, which "seemed unapologetic".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-39)

[Jess Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jess_Phillips "Jess Phillips") announced her candidacy in [Grimsby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grimsby "Grimsby") on 3 January 2020.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-40) She criticised the party's approach to Brexit and [Scottish independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_independence "Scottish independence"), saying that she was opposed to a second referendum on Scottish independence.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Scottish_independence-41) She said that she would be open to arguing for the UK to rejoin the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-42)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-:1-43) Criticising the party's manifesto at the 2019 general election, Phillips said that she would support nationalising railways but would not prioritise further nationalisation.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-:1-43)

Nandy announced that she would stand in a letter to the _[Wigan Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wigan\_Post "Wigan Post")_ on the same day as Phillips.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-44) She argued that the party needed a "bridge" to join areas in [northern England](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northern_England "Northern England") where the party was losing seats and metropolitan areas where the party was gaining support.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Honeycombe-Foster-22)

Starmer, who a poll had indicated was the most popular potential candidate heading into the leadership election, announced his candidacy with a video posted to social media on 4 January followed by a launch in [Stevenage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevenage "Stevenage").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-46)

Long-Bailey announced that she would stand in an article for _[Tribune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tribune\_(magazine) "Tribune (magazine)")_ magazine on 6 January.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-standard1-47) Long-Bailey was seen by many observers and party colleagues as the continuity candidate, who would have continued to take the party in the same direction as Corbyn.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-48)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-49)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-50)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Paul_Mason-51) While she disputed the description,[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-53) her campaign stressed ideological continuity with Corbyn.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-54)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-55) She attracted attention for rating Corbyn "ten out of ten" as a politician,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-56) and called for constitutional reform to spread power more evenly across the country, including abolishing the [House of Lords](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Lords "House of Lords").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Scottish_independence-41)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-57)

### Nominations stage

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Nominations stage")]

Parliamentary
Candidates first needed to receive nominations from at least 5 per cent of the party's MPs and MEPs to progress to the second round of nominations. Starmer won the support of enough MPs and MEPs to progress to the next round of nominations on 8 January, when he was also endorsed by the trade union [Unison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unison_(trade_union) "Unison (trade union)").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-StarmerSufficient-58) The following day, Long-Bailey, Nandy and Phillips gained enough MP and MEP nominations to progress.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-59)

The deadline for PLP and EPLP nominations was 2.30 pm on 13 January.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-60) Lewis, with only five nominations including himself, withdrew from the contest shortly before the deadline.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-lewiswithdrawal-61) Thornberry was also short of the required nominations at the beginning of the day, but managed to obtain enough to qualify less than ten minutes before the deadline, helped by MPs who had formerly nominated Lewis.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5Through-62) After the close of nominations, the party announced that Long-Bailey, Nandy, Phillips, Starmer and Thornberry would proceed to the next stage of the election.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-63) Starmer received 88 nominations, more than any other candidate, followed by Long-Bailey with 33 and Nandy with 31.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-64) Phillips and Thornberry were each nominated by 23 MPs and MEPs, one more than the minimum requirement of 22. Shortly after these nominations were published, Starmer was heavily favoured in the betting odds.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-5Through-62)

Constituencies and affiliates[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ad/Nandy%2C_Starmer_and_Long-Bailey%2C_2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_hustings%2C_Bristol.jpg/250px-Nandy%2C_Starmer_and_Long-Bailey%2C_2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_hustings%2C_Bristol.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nandy,_Starmer_and_Long-Bailey,_2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_hustings,_Bristol.jpg)

Nandy, Starmer and Long-Bailey at the Bristol hustings on 1 February 2020

Corbyn-supporting group [Momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_(organisation) "Momentum (organisation)") balloted its members on a proposal that the group endorse Long-Bailey (alongside Angela Rayner for deputy). Of the 7,395 respondents 70 per cent backed Long-Bailey, but the organisation was criticised by commentators[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-65)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-66)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-67) and by some Momentum members for not giving the option to endorse other candidates.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-68)

Starmer became the first candidate to qualify for the ballot on 20 January with his third affiliate nomination, from the [Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Shop,_Distributive_and_Allied_Workers "Union of Shop, Distributive and Allied Workers");[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-KSMakes-69) by that point, he was also leading in nominations from [Constituency Labour Parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Parties "Constituency Labour Parties") (CLPs). Phillips withdrew from the election on 21 January, saying that she was unable to unite the party.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-JPQuits-70) Nandy became the second candidate to qualify for the ballot on 22 January, having received backing from the GMB and National Union of Mineworkers unions and the Chinese for Labour socialist society.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-NandyQual-71) Long-Bailey was the third candidate to qualify, following further trade union support.

However, Thornberry failed to achieve enough nominations, falling just short of the required number of constituency party nominations and being eliminated on 15 February 2020.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-72)

Reported data breach
The Labour Party reported an alleged breach of data protection rules by Starmer's campaign to the [Information Commissioner's Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_Commissioner's_Office "Information Commissioner's Office") in early February, which it said was in accord with the statutory obligation to report suspected data breaches. The campaign described the complaint as "nonsense". The Starmer campaign chair suggested that the allegations were a result of the Starmer team alerting party officials the week before to a possible data breach by Long-Bailey's campaign, though there was no evidence that this occurred.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-sky-20200211-73)

### Membership ballot

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Membership ballot")]

The first public hustings to feature the final three candidates was held in [Glasgow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glasgow "Glasgow"), [Scotland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scotland "Scotland") on 15 February.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-Scotland_hustings-74)

## Candidates

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Candidates")]

To qualify for the ballot, candidates needed nominations from 10 per cent (22) of the party's [Members of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MPs) and [Members of European Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Members_of_European_Parliament "Members of European Parliament") (MEPs), followed by support from either 5 per cent (33) of [Constituency Labour Parties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituency_Labour_Parties "Constituency Labour Parties") (CLPs), or from at least three affiliated groups, including two trade unions and representing at least 5 per cent of affiliated members. Five candidates ([Rebecca Long-Bailey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Long-Bailey "Rebecca Long-Bailey"), [Lisa Nandy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Nandy "Lisa Nandy"), [Jess Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jess_Phillips "Jess Phillips"), Keir Starmer and [Emily Thornberry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emily_Thornberry "Emily Thornberry")) received sufficient nominations to proceed to the second round of nominations. Starmer had the most nominations from MPs and MEPs at 88, followed by Long-Bailey and Nandy with 33 and 31 nominations respectively. Phillips and Thornberry each received 23 nominations, one above the minimum threshold to proceed.

Three candidates, Long-Bailey, Nandy and Starmer, received sufficient combined support from affiliates and constituency parties to proceed to the final ballot. Starmer received the most nominations from both CLPs and affiliates having received nominations from 374 CLPs and 15 affiliates, followed by Long-Bailey with 164 CLPs and seven affiliates, and finally Nandy with 72 CLPs and four affiliates. The results were announced on 4 April 2020, with Starmer winning the election in the first round with 56.2 per cent of the vote, beating Long-Bailey and Nandy and taking over from Corbyn.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-75)

*   29 January: Long-Bailey receives the required number of nominations to progress to the membership ballot[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-29_January-98)

#### February

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: February")]

*   12 February: The first televised debate is held during a special edition of _[Newsnight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newsnight "Newsnight")_[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-99)
*   15 February: Constituency and affiliate nominations close at midnight; Thornberry fails to receive the required number of nominations and is eliminated
*   24 February: Labour Party members start receiving postal ballots and online voting forms

#### April

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: April")]

*   2 April: Voting closes at midday
*   4 April: Result of the membership ballot announced at 10:45 am.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-100) Keir Starmer declared the new [leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Leader of the Labour Party (UK)")[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-4_April-17) and becomes [Leader of the Opposition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leader_of_the_Opposition_(United_Kingdom) "Leader of the Opposition (United Kingdom)") with 56.2 per cent of ballots cast

## Results

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Results")]

The result of the election as well as the corresponding contest for deputy leader was announced at 10:45 am ([BST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Summer_Time "British Summer Time")) on 4 April 2020. The announcement was originally due to take place at a special conference in London but, due to the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_Kingdom "COVID-19 pandemic in the United Kingdom"), it was cancelled in favour of a "scaled-back event".[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-AnnoCancel-18)

Keir Starmer won the Labour leadership election in the first round of voting.
