**Diane Julie Abbott** (born 27 September 1953) is a British politician who has served as a [Member of Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)") (MP) for [Hackney North and Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_North_and_Stoke_Newington "Hackney North and Stoke Newington") since 1987. She was the first black woman elected to the UK Parliament, and in 2024 became its longest-serving female MP, earning the title [Mother of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_the_House "Mother of the House"). A former [Shadow Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Home_Secretary "Shadow Home Secretary") and [Privy Counsellor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Counsellor "Privy Counsellor"), Abbott has been a prominent figure on the [Labour left](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_left "Labour left") and a vocal campaigner on issues of race and inequality. She was suspended from the Labour Party in 2023 over comments about [racism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism "Racism"), later apologised, and had the [whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whip_(politics) "Whip (politics)") restored ahead of the 2024 general election. In July 2025, she was suspended again after reiterating those remarks in a BBC interview, and sat as an [independent MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Independent_MP "Independent MP") until July 2026, when the whip was restored following the ascension of [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") as Labour leader.

## Early life and career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and career")]

Diane Abbott was born on 27 September 1953 in [Paddington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paddington "Paddington") to [Jamaican](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jamaicans "Jamaicans") parents. Her father was a [welder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welder "Welder") and her mother a nurse.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-nytimes1-3)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-4) Both of her parents left school at the age of 14.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-5) She attended [Harrow County School for Girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrow_County_School_for_Girls "Harrow County School for Girls") (a [grammar school](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grammar_school "Grammar school")) and then [Newnham College, Cambridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newnham_College,_Cambridge "Newnham College, Cambridge"), where she studied history, achieving a lower second-class degree (2:2).[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-FotW-7) At Cambridge, one of her supervisors was [Simon Schama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Schama "Simon Schama").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-8)

After university, Abbott became an administration trainee at the [Home Office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Office "Home Office") (1976 to 1978), and then a Race Relations Officer at the [National Council for Civil Liberties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Council_for_Civil_Liberties "National Council for Civil Liberties") (1978 to 1980).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Vote2001-9) She was a researcher and reporter at [Thames Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thames_Television "Thames Television") from 1980 to 1983, and then a researcher at the breakfast television company [TV-am](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TV-am "TV-am") from 1983 to 1985.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Voice-10) She was a press officer at the [Greater London Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_London_Council "Greater London Council") under [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone") from 1985 to 1986, and Head of Press and Public Relations at [Lambeth Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lambeth_Council "Lambeth Council") from 1986 to 1987.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Vote2001-9)

In 2024, during the [Undercover Policing Inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undercover_Policing_Inquiry "Undercover Policing Inquiry") into the conduct of about 139 undercover police officers who infiltrated and disrupted social justice groups, the [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police") apologised for using undercover officers to spy on anti-racism campaigners, including Abbott, during the 1980s and 1990s. Many secret police reports on Abbott were uncovered by the inquiry. Abbott criticised these activities as being racist and unjustified.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-guardian-20240703-11)

Abbott's career in politics began in 1982 when she was elected to [Westminster City Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Westminster_City_Council "Westminster City Council"), serving until 1986. In 1983, she was active in the [Labour Party Black Sections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_Black_Sections "Labour Party Black Sections") movement, alongside [Bernie Grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernie_Grant "Bernie Grant"), [Paul Boateng](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Boateng "Paul Boateng") and [Keith Vaz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Vaz "Keith Vaz"), campaigning for greater African Caribbean and Asian political representation.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Voice-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Bush-12) In 1985, she sought to be selected in [Brent East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brent_East "Brent East"), losing out to [Ken Livingstone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ken_Livingstone "Ken Livingstone").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-13)

## Parliamentary career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Parliamentary career")]

At the [1987 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_United_Kingdom_general_election "1987 United Kingdom general election"), Abbott was elected to Parliament as MP for [Hackney North and Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_North_and_Stoke_Newington "Hackney North and Stoke Newington"), winning with 48.7% of the vote and a majority of 7,678.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-14) She was the first black woman to become an MP.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-15)

Abbott has served on a number of [parliamentary committees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_committee "Parliamentary committee") on social and international issues and held [shadow ministerial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_minister "Shadow minister") positions in successive [shadow cabinets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_cabinet "Shadow cabinet"). For most of the 1990s, she also served on the [Treasury Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treasury_Select_Committee "Treasury Select Committee") of the House of Commons.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-hackneycitizen.co.uk-16) She went on to serve on the [Foreign Affairs Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Affairs_Select_Committee "Foreign Affairs Select Committee").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-hackneycitizen.co.uk-16) She gave birth to her son in October 1991, one year before the House of Commons introduced a crèche.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:2-17)

At the [1992 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_United_Kingdom_general_election "1992 United Kingdom general election"), Abbott was re-elected as MP for Hackney North and Stoke Newington with an increased vote share of 57.8% and an increased majority of 10,727.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-18) She was again re-elected at the [1997 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_United_Kingdom_general_election "1997 United Kingdom general election") with an increased vote share of 65.2% and an increased majority of 15,627.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-19) She was again re-elected at the [2001 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_United_Kingdom_general_election "2001 United Kingdom general election"), with a decreased vote share of 61% and a decreased majority of 13,651.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-20) She was again re-elected at the [2005 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_United_Kingdom_general_election "2005 United Kingdom general election"), with a decreased vote share of 48.6% and a decreased majority of 7,427.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-21)

Abbott's speech on civil liberties, in the debate on the [Counter-Terrorism Bill 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counter-Terrorism_Bill_2008 "Counter-Terrorism Bill 2008"),[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-22) won _[The Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Spectator "The Spectator")_ magazine's "Parliamentary Speech of the Year" award,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-23) and further recognition at the 2008 Human Rights awards.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-24)

Abbott chairs the All-Party Parliamentary British-Caribbean Group and the All-Party Sickle Cell and Thalassemia Group.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-hackneycitizen.co.uk-16) She is the founder of the London Schools and the Black Child initiative, which aims to raise educational achievement levels amongst black children.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-25)

At the [2010 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_United_Kingdom_general_election "2010 United Kingdom general election"), Abbott was again re-elected, with an increased vote share of 55% and an increased majority of 14,461.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-26)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-27)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-28)

At [Goldsmiths' College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goldsmiths'_College "Goldsmiths' College"), on 26 October 2012, a jubilee celebration was held to honour Abbott's 25 years in Parliament, with participants in a series of contributions including [Herman Ouseley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herman_Ouseley "Herman Ouseley"), [Linton Kwesi Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linton_Kwesi_Johnson "Linton Kwesi Johnson"), [Kadija Sesay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kadija_Sesay "Kadija Sesay"), [Aminatta Forna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aminatta_Forna "Aminatta Forna"), [Shami Chakrabarti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shami_Chakrabarti "Shami Chakrabarti"), [SuAndi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SuAndi "SuAndi"), [Yvonne Brewster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yvonne_Brewster "Yvonne Brewster"), [Malika Booker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malika_Booker "Malika Booker"), [Zena Edwards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zena_Edwards "Zena Edwards") and others.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-D-Day-30)

At the [2015 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_United_Kingdom_general_election "2015 United Kingdom general election"), Abbott was again re-elected with an increased vote share of 62.9% and an increased majority of 24,008.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-electoralcalculus-31)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-32) At the snap [2017 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election"), she was again re-elected with an increased vote share of 75.1% and an increased majority of 35,139.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-34)

A speech by Abbott in a House of Commons debate on the Caribbean is included in [Margaret Busby](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margaret_Busby "Margaret Busby")'s 2019 anthology _[New Daughters of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Daughters\_of\_Africa "New Daughters of Africa")_.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-36)

At the [2019 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_United_Kingdom_general_election "2019 United Kingdom general election"), Abbott was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 70.3% and a decreased majority of 33,188.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-37)

At the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election") held on 4 July, Abbott was re-elected with a vote share of 60%.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-BBCresults-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Voice_results-39)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-40)

Abbott was given the honorific title [Mother of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mother_of_the_House "Mother of the House") as the longest continuously serving female MP,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-41) delivering her first speech in that role on 9 July 2024, when she congratulated new MPs and said: "It is a great job and you will never regret coming here. ... When I was a new member in 1987, there were only 40 female members of Parliament. Today we have 264, and some of us are glad that we have lived to see this. And I can't speak about the increased numbers of female members of Parliament without referencing my predecessor Baroness [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman"), who did so much to work to have an equal and diverse House."[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-42)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-43) Tributes were paid to Abbott by [Speaker of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_(United_Kingdom) "Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)") Sir [Lindsay Hoyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindsay_Hoyle "Lindsay Hoyle"), as well as by Prime Minister Keir Starmer.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-44)

### 2010 leadership election and frontbench role

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2010 leadership election and frontbench role")]

Main article: [2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3a/Diane_Abbott%2C_New_Statesman_hustings.jpg/250px-Diane_Abbott%2C_New_Statesman_hustings.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diane_Abbott,_New_Statesman_hustings.jpg)

Abbott speaking at the _[New Statesman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New\_Statesman "New Statesman")_ hustings for the [2010 Labour Party leadership election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2010 Labour Party leadership election (UK)")

On 20 May 2010, Abbott announced her intention to stand in the Labour leadership contest. She secured the necessary 33 nominations, assisted by the withdrawal of [John McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McDonnell "John McDonnell") and support from [David Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Miliband "David Miliband") and [Jack Straw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Straw "Jack Straw"), among others.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-NextRound-45)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-46) On 25 September 2010, [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") was announced as the new leader of the Labour Party, Abbott having been eliminated in the first round of voting after securing 7.24% of votes.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Kite-47)

Abbott was later appointed Shadow Minister for Public Health by [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband"), taking shadow responsibility for a range of issues including children's health, maternity services, sexual health, tobacco, nursing, obesity and alcohol abuse.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-48) Following her move onto the front bench, the _[Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph "The Daily Telegraph")_ said on 27 September 2011 that Abbott had "become one of Labour's best front bench performers".[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-49)

On the issue of [abortion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion "Abortion"), Abbott has become a vocal "[pro-choice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pro-choice "Pro-choice")" supporter, opposing moves towards changing abortion counselling policy, and reducing the abortion time limit. She resigned from a cross-party group on abortion counselling, saying it was no more than a front to push forward an anti-abortion agenda without debate in parliament.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-50)

In 2011, she voted in favour of [military intervention in Libya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_intervention_in_Libya "Military intervention in Libya").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-51)

On 5 February 2013, following the Second Reading, Abbott voted in favour of the [Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Same_Sex_Couples)_Bill "Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Bill").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-52)

### Removal from the frontbench and 2015 London mayoral election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Removal from the frontbench and 2015 London mayoral election")]

Main article: [2015 London Labour Party mayoral selection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Labour_Party_mayoral_selection "2015 London Labour Party mayoral selection")

On 8 October 2013, Abbott was sacked as Shadow Public Health Minister in a reshuffle by Labour leader [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-53) and replaced by [Luciana Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luciana_Berger "Luciana Berger").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-54) On 23 June 2014, Abbott had stated she would consider standing in the [2016 London mayoral election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_mayoral_election "2016 London mayoral election");[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-standard-20140623-55) on 30 November 2014, Abbott announced her intention to put herself forward to become Labour's candidate in the election,[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-56) but was unsuccessful in the [2015 nomination process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Labour_Party_mayoral_selection "2015 London Labour Party mayoral selection").

She was one of 16 signatories of an open letter to [Ed Miliband](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ed_Miliband "Ed Miliband") in January 2015 calling on the party to commit to oppose further austerity, take rail franchises back into public ownership and strengthen collective bargaining arrangements.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-57)

### Return to the frontbench

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Return to the frontbench")]

A close ally of [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"), Abbott was one of 36 Labour MPs to nominate him as a candidate in the [Labour leadership election of 2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2015 Labour Party leadership election (UK)").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-58) Following Corbyn's election as Labour leader, Abbott was appointed to the post of [Shadow Secretary of State for International Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Secretary_of_State_for_International_Development "Shadow Secretary of State for International Development").[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-59)

On 27 June 2016, following the [resignations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_British_shadow_cabinet_resignations "2016 British shadow cabinet resignations") of many of Labour's shadow ministerial team in the aftermath of the [Brexit referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brexit_referendum "Brexit referendum"), Abbott was promoted to the position of [Shadow Health Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Health_Secretary "Shadow Health Secretary").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-60)

On 6 October 2016, following the resignation of [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham"), Abbott was appointed [Shadow Home Secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Home_Secretary "Shadow Home Secretary"). Following the Article 50 vote in February 2017, Abbott was involved in a [controversy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Diane_Abbott%E2%80%93David_Davis_controversy "2017 Diane Abbott–David Davis controversy") with fellow MP [David Davis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Diane_Abbott%E2%80%93David_Davis_controversy "2017 Diane Abbott–David Davis controversy").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-61)

She was sworn of the [Privy Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privy_Council_(United_Kingdom) "Privy Council (United Kingdom)") on 15 February 2017.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-62)

### 2017 general election

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2017 general election")]

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Diane_Abbot_Corbyn_leadership_rally_August_2016.jpg/250px-Diane_Abbot_Corbyn_leadership_rally_August_2016.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diane_Abbot_Corbyn_leadership_rally_August_2016.jpg)

Abbott at a [Jeremy Corbyn leadership](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK) "2016 Labour Party leadership election (UK)") rally in August 2016

On 2 May 2017, during [that year's general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_general_election "2017 United Kingdom general election") campaign, Labour's pledge to recruit an extra 10,000 police officers was overshadowed by Abbott's inability to give accurate [funding figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funding "Funding"). In an interview on [LBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LBC "LBC") Radio with [Nick Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Ferrari "Nick Ferrari"), she repeatedly struggled to explain how the promise would be funded. In the interview, Abbott frequently paused, shuffled her papers and gave out the wrong [figures](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Number "Number").[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-63) When asked about her performance, the Labour leader, [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"), insisted he was not embarrassed by what many pundits called a "[car crash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_crash "Car crash")" [interview](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interview "Interview").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-64)

In a further interview conducted by [ITV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ITV_(TV_network) "ITV (TV network)") on 5 May 2017, as the [2017 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2017 United Kingdom local elections") results were being announced, Abbott was again unable to give accurate figures on the Labour Party's performance suggesting that the party had a net loss of 50 seats. However, her figure was corrected by the interviewer who stated that Labour had in fact lost 125 seats, at which point Abbott said that the last figures she had seen were a net loss of around 100.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-65)

Appearing on [Andrew Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marr "Andrew Marr")'s Sunday morning programme for the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") on 28 May, Abbott's apparent support for the IRA nearly 35 years ago came up, along with some parliamentary votes Marr thought questionable. These included her advocacy of the abolition of "conspiratorial groups" such as [MI5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MI5 "MI5") and [Special Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Branch_(Metropolitan_Police) "Special Branch (Metropolitan Police)") in the late 1980s, both of which she said had been successfully reformed. She defended a vote opposing the proscription of a list of groups, including [al-Qaeda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Qaeda "Al-Qaeda"), on the basis that some of the others had the status of dissidents in their country of origin and Abbott would have voted to ban al-Qaeda in isolation.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-66) According to [Sam Coates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Coates "Sam Coates") in _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_, this appearance was arranged without the consent of Labour's campaign team.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Coates030617-67)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/Diane_Abbott_%2825795818902%29.jpg/250px-Diane_Abbott_%2825795818902%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Diane_Abbott_(25795818902).jpg)

Abbott at a rally in [Trafalgar Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trafalgar_Square "Trafalgar Square") in 2016

On 5 June 2017, during a [Sky News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sky_News "Sky News") interview, Abbott was unable to answer questions about the Harris report on how to protect London from terror attacks. She insisted that she had read the report, but was unable to recall any of the 127 recommendations. When asked if she could remember the specific recommendations, Abbott said: "I think it was an important review and we should act on it."[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-68)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-69) Abbott also denied reports that Corbyn and shadow chancellor [John McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McDonnell "John McDonnell") were attempting to stop her from making broadcasts.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Coates030617-67)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-70) The next day, Abbott withdrew at the last minute – citing illness – from a joint interview on _[Woman's Hour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woman's\_Hour "Woman's Hour")_ on 6 June, in which she had been due to face her Conservative frontbench opposite number [Amber Rudd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amber_Rudd "Amber Rudd").[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-71) On 7 June, Corbyn announced that Abbott was "not well" and had stepped aside in her role as Shadow Home Secretary. [Lyn Brown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyn_Brown "Lyn Brown") was temporarily assigned to replace her.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Walker-72)[Barry Gardiner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barry_Gardiner "Barry Gardiner") said in a radio interview on LBC that Abbott had been diagnosed with having a "long-term" medical condition, and was "coming to terms with that".[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Walker-72)

The following week it became known that Abbott had been diagnosed with [type 2 diabetes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Type_2_diabetes "Type 2 diabetes") in 2015.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Asthana-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-BBC_News-74) "During the election campaign, everything went crazy – and the diabetes was out of control, the blood sugar was out of control", she told _[The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Guardian "The Guardian")_.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Asthana-73) Dealing with six or seven interviews in a row became problematic because she was not eating enough food, which forced a break upon her; however, the condition is back under control.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Asthana-73) Abbott returned to the role of Shadow Home Secretary on 18 June.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-75)

### 2017–2023

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2017–2023")]

On 2 October 2019, Abbott became the first black MP at the dispatch box at [Prime Minister's Questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister's_Questions "Prime Minister's Questions").[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-76) She served as a temporary [stand-in](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stand-in "Stand-in") for the Leader of the Opposition, [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn"), while [First Secretary of State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Secretary_of_State "First Secretary of State")[Dominic Raab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dominic_Raab "Dominic Raab") stood in for Prime Minister [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson").[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-77)

Abbott was a supporter of [Speaker of the House of Commons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_(United_Kingdom) "Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)")[John Bercow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Bercow "John Bercow"), and defended him from bullying allegations made by [David Leakey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Leakey "David Leakey").[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-78)

On 23 February 2020, Abbott said she would be standing down as Shadow Home Secretary and leaving the [frontbench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Official_Opposition_frontbench "Official Opposition frontbench")[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-79) upon the election of a new Labour leader. She stood down on 5 April and was succeeded by [Nick Thomas-Symonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Thomas-Symonds "Nick Thomas-Symonds").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-80)

In April 2020, she was appointed to the [Home Affairs Select Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Home_Affairs_Select_Committee "Home Affairs Select Committee").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-81)

In May 2021, she wrote in a _Guardian_ article that if Labour were to lose the [Batley and Spen by-election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Batley_and_Spen_by-election "2021 Batley and Spen by-election"), Starmer should resign as Labour leader.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-82) She described the [local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2021 United Kingdom local elections") as disappointing for Labour. Abbott criticised the [shadow cabinet reshuffle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/May_2021_British_shadow_cabinet_reshuffle "May 2021 British shadow cabinet reshuffle") later carried out by Keir Starmer. She told [Sophy Ridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sophy_Ridge "Sophy Ridge") on Sky News that his demotion of [Angela Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Rayner "Angela Rayner") was "baffling".[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-83) Following the [2022 local elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_United_Kingdom_local_elections "2022 United Kingdom local elections"), Abbott said that Keir Starmer should resign if he is fined by [Durham Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Durham_Constabulary "Durham Constabulary") over [Beergate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beergate "Beergate").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-84)

On 24 February 2022, Abbott was one of eleven Labour MPs who signed a statement by the [Stop the War Coalition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stop_the_War_Coalition "Stop the War Coalition") criticising the UK government for "sabre-rattling" over [Russia’s invasion of Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia%E2%80%99s_invasion_of_Ukraine "Russia’s invasion of Ukraine") and for saying Ukraine has a right to join NATO if it wishes. The statement called on NATO to stop its "eastward expansion and commit to a new security deal for Europe". All eleven MPs subsequently removed their signatures after being threatened with losing the [whip](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whip_(politics) "Whip (politics)").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-85)

### April 2023: Whip removed

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: April 2023: Whip removed")]

In April 2023, Abbott wrote[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-86) to _[The Observer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Observer "The Observer")_ in response to an article on racism faced by Irish people, Jewish people and [Travellers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irish_Travellers "Irish Travellers"), saying they do not experience racism as black people do.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:4-87) Labour withdrew the whip following its publication.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:4-87) Abbott withdrew her remarks, apologised and said: "Racism takes many forms, and it is completely undeniable that Jewish people have suffered its monstrous effects, as have Irish people, Travellers and many others."[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-88) Abbott also said the letter was an initial draft sent by mistake.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-89) According to _[The Jewish Chronicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jewish\_Chronicle "The Jewish Chronicle")_, the letter had been sent twice.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-90)

In September 2023, Abbott, still suspended, said that she had realised that "As a Black woman, I will not get a fair hearing from this Labour leadership".[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-91)

The Labour Party National Executive Committee concluded its inquiry into her comments in December 2023 and issued her with a "formal warning" for "engaging in conduct that was, in the opinion of the NEC, prejudicial and grossly detrimental to the Labour Party". She was also directed to complete an online e-learning module, which she did in February 2024.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Standard_28-5-24-92) The campaign group [Momentum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Momentum_(organisation) "Momentum (organisation)") criticised the Labour Party and Starmer for failing to restore the whip to Abbott once she had completed the module.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Standard_28-5-24-92)

### Frank Hester

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Frank Hester")]

On 11 March 2024, _The Guardian_ alleged that businessman and [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") donor [Frank Hester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Hester "Frank Hester") had said in 2019 that Abbott made him "want to hate all black women" and that "she should be shot".[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Zeffman-93) Hester apologised to Abbott on [X](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter") (previously Twitter) after the allegations were published, stating that his comments were "rude" and had "nothing to do with her gender nor colour of skin". The comments led to Labour and the [Liberal Democrats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Democrats_(UK) "Liberal Democrats (UK)") calling on the Conservative Party to return Hester's £10 million donation.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:5-94)[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-95) Abbott described Hester's remarks as "frightening" and reported Hester to the [Metropolitan Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Police "Metropolitan Police")'s parliamentary liaison and investigations team.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Zeffman-93)[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-96)

On 13 March 2024, Abbott criticised the [Speaker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Speaker_of_the_House_of_Commons_(United_Kingdom) "Speaker of the House of Commons (United Kingdom)") of the House of Commons ([Sir Lindsay Hoyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Lindsay_Hoyle "Sir Lindsay Hoyle")) after he failed to call on her to speak during [Prime Minister's Questions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister's_Questions "Prime Minister's Questions"), which was dominated by the "race row" surrounding her. It was reported that Abbott stood up 46 times in 35 minutes to try to have her say, without success. She later criticised the Speaker, saying: "I don't know whose interests the Speaker thinks he is serving. But it is not the interests of the Commons or democracy."[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:5-94)

### 2024: Whip restored

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 2024: Whip restored")]

Abbott did receive some support from Labour Party MPs. [Deputy Leader of the Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deputy_Leader_of_the_Labour_Party_(UK) "Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (UK)")[Angela Rayner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Rayner "Angela Rayner") said she hoped for Abbott to have the whip restored.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-97) On 17 March, a former deputy leader of the party, [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman"), said she would be sad if Abbott's career ended without her being readmitted to the [Parliamentary Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliamentary_Labour_Party "Parliamentary Labour Party").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-98) At a rally in support of Abbott, Jeremy Corbyn criticised the Labour Party for "using [Abbott's] image and story as a way of trying to raise money for the Labour party while at the same time not recognising the injustice of her removal from the parliamentary Labour party".[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-99)

The Labour Party restored the whip to Abbott on 28 May 2024. The following day Abbott said that she has been barred by the Labour Party from standing as a Labour Party candidate at the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election").[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-ind290524-100) Starmer said that no decision had yet been taken.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-101)[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-102)

On 30 May, an open letter signed by many prominent Black British figures (including [Lenny Henry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lenny_Henry "Lenny Henry"), [David Harewood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Harewood "David Harewood"), [Reni Eddo-Lodge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reni_Eddo-Lodge "Reni Eddo-Lodge"), [Misan Harriman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misan_Harriman "Misan Harriman"), [Afua Hirsch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afua_Hirsch "Afua Hirsch"), [Jackie Kay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackie_Kay "Jackie Kay"), [Linton Kwesi Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linton_Kwesi_Johnson "Linton Kwesi Johnson"), [Adrian Lester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Lester "Adrian Lester") and [Gary Younge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Younge "Gary Younge")) claimed that the Labour Party's indecisiveness about Abbott's future was an example "of the systemic racism highlighted in the [Forde report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forde_Report "Forde Report") on factionalism in the Labour party commissioned by Starmer himself".[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-103)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-104)

Starmer said on 31 May that Abbott would be "free" to stand as a Labour candidate.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:6-105)

On 2 June 2024, Abbott tweeted that she was now the Labour candidate for [Hackney North and Stoke Newington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hackney_North_and_Stoke_Newington "Hackney North and Stoke Newington") at the general election.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-106)[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-107)

At the [2024 general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_Kingdom_general_election "2024 United Kingdom general election") held on 4 July, Abbott was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 59.5% and a decreased majority of 15,080.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-108)

### 2025: Whip removed for the second time

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: 2025: Whip removed for the second time")]

On 17 July 2025, Abbott was suspended from the Labour Party following remarks made during a BBC interview in which she reiterated comments about racism that had previously led to her suspension in 2023.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-109) In July 2025, senior Labour Party sources told _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_ that Abbott was unlikely to be readmitted to the Party.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-110) She continued to sit as an independent MP, saying: "It is obvious this Labour leadership wants me out."[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-111)

### 2026: Whip restored for the second time

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: 2026: Whip restored for the second time")]

The whip was restored for Abbott in July 2026 following the ascension of [Andy Burnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Burnham "Andy Burnham") as Labour leader.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-112)

In September 2026, Abbott, along with [Jeremy Corbyn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeremy_Corbyn "Jeremy Corbyn") and all 5 [Green Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_Party_of_England_and_Wales "Green Party of England and Wales") MPs, was banned from entering Israel.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-113)

## Media work

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Media work")]

Until her appointment as a shadow minister in October 2010, Abbott appeared alongside media personality and former Conservative politician [Michael Portillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Portillo "Michael Portillo") on the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC")'s weekly politics digest _[This Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Week\_(2003\_TV\_programme) "This Week (2003 TV programme)")_. Abbott and Portillo have known each other since their schooldays, during which they appeared in joint school productions of _[Romeo and Juliet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romeo\_and\_Juliet "Romeo and Juliet")_ (although not in the title roles), and of _[Macbeth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macbeth "Macbeth")_ as [Lady Macduff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Macduff "Lady Macduff") and [Macduff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Macduff_(Macbeth) "Macduff (Macbeth)") respectively.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-114)

In August 2012, the BBC Trust ruled that payments to Abbott for her appearances on _This Week_ were made in breach of BBC guidelines that banned payments to MPs who were representing their political parties. For her part, Abbott had correctly declared the payments in the Parliamentary Register of Members' Interests. The Trust also said that Abbott had appeared on the show too often.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-115)

Abbott is a frequent public speaker,[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-116) newspaper contributor[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-117) and TV performer, appearing on programmes including _[Have I Got News for You](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Have\_I\_Got\_News\_for\_You "Have I Got News for You")_,[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-118)_Celebrity [Come Dine with Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Come\_Dine\_with\_Me "Come Dine with Me")_[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-119) and _[Cash in the Celebrity Attic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cash\_in\_the\_Celebrity\_Attic "Cash in the Celebrity Attic")_.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-120)

Abbott was shortlisted for the [Grassroot Diplomat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grassroot_Diplomat "Grassroot Diplomat") Initiative Award in 2015 for her work on London Schools and the Black Child, and remains in the directory of the _Grassroot Diplomat Who's Who_ publication.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-121)

Abbott has a record of differing from some party policies, voting against the [Iraq War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War "Iraq War"),[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-tcs.cam.ac.uk-122) opposing [ID cards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ID_cards "ID cards") and campaigning against the [renewal of Britain's Trident nuclear weapons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trident_(UK_nuclear_programme)#Renewal "Trident (UK nuclear programme)").[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Riddell-123)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-bbc.co.uk-124)

### Abortion rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Abortion rights")]

Abbott supported a number of amendments to the [Human Fertilisation and Embryology Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_Fertilisation_and_Embryology_Act_2008 "Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 2008") (now Act) that favoured [abortion rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_rights "Abortion rights")[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Galbraith-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:0-126) (along with [Katy Clark](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Katy_Clark "Katy Clark") MP and [John McDonnell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_McDonnell "John McDonnell") MP)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-127) – including in 2008 leading on the NC30 Amendment of the Abortion Act 1967: Application to Northern Ireland.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-128) Writing for _The Guardian_, Abbott argued that

> When it comes to the right to choose, women in Northern Ireland are second-class citizens. They are denied the NHS treatment and funding for abortion that is permitted to every other woman in the United Kingdom.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-129)

It was reported that the Labour Government at the time (in particular [Harriet Harman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harriet_Harman "Harriet Harman")[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Galbraith-125)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-:0-126)) asked MPs not to table these pro-abortion amendments (and at least until [Third Reading](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Reading "Third Reading")) and then allegedly used parliamentary mechanisms in order to prevent a vote accordingly.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Galbraith-125) Speaking in the debate in Parliament, Abbott criticised these "manoeuvres":

> I speak against the programme motion because—and I say this with no pleasure—it and the order of discussion appear to be a shabby manoeuvre by Ministers to stop the full debate of some very important matters. I appreciate that Ministers did not intend this to be a Bill about abortion. I am open to the argument that we should have another piece of legislation that would enable a full debate on most of the matters in relation to abortion that have been raised as amendments and new clauses to the Bill, but there is a special case for debating and voting on the particular new clause that I tabled to extend the 1967 Act to Northern Ireland.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-130)

### Saudi Arabia

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Saudi Arabia")]

Abbott criticised [David Cameron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Cameron "David Cameron")'s government for its continued support for [Saudi Arabian-led military intervention in Yemen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saudi_Arabian-led_intervention_in_Yemen "Saudi Arabian-led intervention in Yemen"). In March 2016, Abbott wrote: "over the past year alone, Britain has sold around £6bn worth of weapons to Saudi Arabia, whose campaign in Yemen is targeting civilians – 191 such attacks have collectively been reported by the UN, HRW and Amnesty."[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-131)

### European Union

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: European Union")]

Abbott voted against the [Maastricht Treaty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht_Treaty "Maastricht Treaty").[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-132)

Abbott campaigned and supported the Labour Party's official preference for the remain campaign in the [2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_United_Kingdom_European_Union_membership_referendum "2016 United Kingdom European Union membership referendum").[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-133)[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-134) In December 2016, she told [Andrew Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marr "Andrew Marr") that Labour policy was to respect the result of the referendum.[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-135)

In January 2017, Abbott stated that Labour could oppose the bill to trigger [Article 50](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_from_the_European_Union "Withdrawal from the European Union") if Labour's amendments were rejected.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-136) She abstained from voting on the second reading of the [Brexit Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union_(Notification_of_Withdrawal)_Act_2017 "European Union (Notification of Withdrawal) Act 2017"), after becoming ill hours before the vote,[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-137) and later voted in favour at the third and final reading. She said she did this out of party loyalty and respect for democracy.[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-138) In December 2017, Abbott did not support holding a [second referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proposed_referendum_on_the_Brexit_withdrawal_agreement "Proposed referendum on the Brexit withdrawal agreement"),[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-139) saying in 2018 that the UK would vote to leave again in a hypothetical poll.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-140) She supported the holding of one following the [2019 European Parliament elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_European_Parliament_election_in_the_United_Kingdom "2019 European Parliament election in the United Kingdom").[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-141) She consistently voted against the [withdrawal agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_agreement "Withdrawal agreement").[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-142)

### Windrush scandal

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Windrush scandal")]

Abbott wrote to [Sajid Javid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sajid_Javid "Sajid Javid") demanding that he publish the figures for people caught up in the [Windrush scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Windrush_scandal "Windrush scandal"), and also tell how many Commonwealth citizens lost their jobs, became homeless and were prevented from using public services. She wrote that "warm words are not enough", and maintained that transparency was needed to give the Windrush generation confidence ministers have come to grips with what is

> ...clearly a systemic problem at the Home Office. In order to make good on your promise to do right by the Windrush generation and begin to right this historic wrong, you must stop covering up the extent of the Windrush crisis and publish these figures. (...) It is unacceptable and frankly scandalous that the extent of the Windrush crisis is yet to be revealed and that the home secretary is still to publish these figures. As the Windrush scandal shows, the hostile environment inevitably catches our fellow citizens who are legally entitled to be here in its net. The government now needs to stop covering up the true human cost of the hostile environment.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-145)

In August 2018, Abbott complained that there were still delays in settling Windrush claims, saying: "From the Windrush scandal to immigration detention, to these outrageous delays – it is long past time that the government takes responsibility for leaving people distressed and destitute."[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-146)

### Comments about Mao Zedong

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Comments about Mao Zedong")]

In 2008, during a BBC One _[This Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/This\_Week\_(2003\_TV\_programme) "This Week (2003 TV programme)")_ interview between Abbott, [Michael Portillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Portillo "Michael Portillo") and [Andrew Neil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Neil "Andrew Neil"), Abbott said about the Chinese leader [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"): "I suppose some people will judge that on balance Mao did more good than harm... He led his country from feudalism, he helped to defeat the Japanese and he left his country on the verge of the great economic success they are having now." She finished by saying: "I was just putting the case for Mao."[[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-147)[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-148)

### Assisted dying

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Assisted dying")]

In November 2024, Abbott said she would not support [Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminally_Ill_Adults_(End_of_Life)_Bill "Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill") on assisted dying for terminally ill people.[[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-149) She also criticised the amount of time available for scrutiny of the bill, brought by Labour backbencher [Kim Leadbeater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kim_Leadbeater "Kim Leadbeater"). She co-wrote a piece in [The Guardian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guardian "The Guardian") with [Father of the House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Father_of_the_House_(United_Kingdom) "Father of the House (United Kingdom)") Conservative MP [Edward Leigh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Leigh "Edward Leigh") opposing the [assisted suicide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assisted_suicide_in_the_United_Kingdom "Assisted suicide in the United Kingdom") bill.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-150)

### Northern Ireland

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Diane_Abbott&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Northern Ireland")]

In May 2017, _[The Sunday Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Times "The Sunday Times")_ reported that Abbott called for the withdrawal of British troops and Irish reunification in a 1984 interview with _Labour and Ireland_, a pro-republican journal.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Gilligan-151)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-152) In the 1984 interview, Abbott criticised the Unionist population of Northern Ireland as an "enclave of white supremacist ideology comparable to white settlers in Zimbabwe", and called for their views to be ignored on the question of [Unification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Ireland "United Ireland"), adding: "Ireland is our struggle—every defeat of the British state is a victory for all of us. A defeat in Northern Ireland would be a defeat indeed."[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Gilligan-151)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-Gilliganblog-153) In May 2017, while Shadow Home Secretary, she was asked by [Andrew Marr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Marr "Andrew Marr") whether she regretted her comments. Abbott replied that "It was 34 years ago. I've moved on."[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diane_Abbott#cite_note-154)
